title: Implementing Learning Principles with a Personal AI Tutor: A Case Study
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a personal AI tutor can improve learning by operationalizing well-established learning-science principles such as personalization, retrieval practice, and spaced repetition. The authors ask whether students who actively use the tutor perform better academically, and whether the system’s internal model of each learner’s knowledge meaningfully tracks actual performance.

The intervention was a mobile and web-based AI tutor that used GPT-3 to generate 800 microlearning questions from course materials before the semester began. The app then used a neural-network model to predict each student’s probability of answering each question correctly and to schedule personalized retrieval practice at an adaptive difficulty level. A visual “learnet” also showed students their estimated grasp of course concepts. The study was implemented over one semester in an online bachelor-level psychology neuroscience course at UniDistance Suisse, with a parallel neuroanatomy course and Moodle quizzes used as comparison contexts.

Results showed that students who actively engaged with the AI tutor earned higher final exam grades than inactive students, and that active users improved their rank relative to a parallel course without the tutor. By contrast, activity on Moodle quizzes did not show a similarly consistent advantage. The predicted grasp from the neural network correlated strongly with exam grades among regular users, suggesting that the model captured meaningful knowledge variation. The authors conclude that personal AI tutors can support learning when they are tightly aligned with learning-science principles, though the evidence is correlational and not based on random assignment.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an observational case study with no random assignment or active control group, so internal validity is limited. The authors triangulate with a parallel course and Moodle quizzes, but the design remains correlational/quasi-experimental rather than a strong causal evaluation.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported academic effects are medium-to-large in magnitude (e.g., d=0.69 and d=0.73; percentile gains of about 12-18 points), suggesting potentially meaningful impact. However, the evidence comes from a small higher-education sample in a single course, so generalizability to middle school math is uncertain.

interventions.use_case: Personal AI tutor app that used GPT-3 to generate microlearning questions from neuroscience course materials and adaptively selected retrieval-practice items based on a neural-network model of each student's grasp.

Personalized learning platform that modeled each learner's knowledge state and adapted spacing, difficulty, and question selection to maintain desirable difficulty and individualized retrieval practice.
Mobile and web microlearning app delivering bite-sized question practice across a semester, with concept-linked feedback and a visual 'learnet' progress display.
AI tutor system providing personalized, adaptive question sequencing and feedback using predicted mastery/grasp to simulate one-on-one tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: Active users of the AI tutor earned higher final exam grades than inactive users in the main course. The average grade difference was 0.71 points on a 1-6 scale, with an average Cohen's d of 0.69 across activity thresholds; the analysis used n=51 exam takers and independent t-tests.
finding.measure: Final course exam grade (1-6 scale) comparing active vs inactive AI tutor users
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.08 for grade-difference estimate; group SD not reported

finding.finding_summary: In a within-student comparison against a parallel course without the AI tutor, active users improved their relative standing more on the main course exam. Among students taking both exams (n=47), active users gained 18.1 more percentile points than inactive students; active students gained 12.4 percentile points on average versus -5.7 for inactive students, with t(45)=2.33 and Cohen's d=0.73.
finding.measure: Percentile rank change from parallel course exam to main course exam

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests the AI tutor's 'learnet' and adaptive difficulty were designed to support engagement and motivation, but these were not directly measured with validated instruments. Evidence here is indirect, based on usage patterns (mean 1800 answers, 7.2 hours across 26 days among users) rather than a direct motivational or self-regulation outcome.
finding.measure: Usage/engagement with the AI tutor app
finding.study_size: n=43 linked users among 51 exam takers
finding.std_deviation: Answers SD=2700; hours SD=10; days SD=31
